newsitem.title: UK: Oil edges higher with U.S. gasoline demand.
newsitem.headline: Oil edges higher with U.S. gasoline demand.

text.p: Oil prices ticked up again on Wednesday without showing any sign of shifting from the tight range which has smothered crude trade since early June.
London futures for benchmark Brent blend rose 17 cents a barrel to close at $18.39.
Brent has remained above $18 despite the threat of a deluge of Iraqi exports within the next few weeks when Baghdad is expected to implement the second phase of its U.N. oil-for-food deal.
Traders attribute the market resilience to strong petroleum product demand in western markets, combined with recent supply disruptions.
"We've had the losses in Colombian supplies and bad weather in the Gulf of Mexico while product demand in the U.S. is on fire again," said a trader in London.
Latest U.S. inventory data, released after markets closed on Tuesday by the American Petroleum Institute (API), showed gasoline stocks dropping 2.8 million barrels.
But a rise in crude stocks countered some of the impact of the gasoline stockdraw.
Countering the decline in refined product stocks was a 1.4 million barrel build in crude stocks reported by the API when dealers had forecasted a one- to two-million barrel decline.
The crude stock build comes when the market is already bracing for the resumption of Iraqi crude exports.
The review of Iraq aid distribution for restarting oil sales is expected to be completed by the end of July, U.N. diplomats said Tuesday.
Dealers expect Iraqi oil sales will restart at a brisk pace some time in August, though the extent of sales may depend on whether buyers come forward willingly and at what price the oil is offered.

By early August Iraq will have only about a month to sell an initial $1 billion tranche which, at current prices, would require a burst of exports at some two million bpd, probably in excess of Iraqi export capacity.
